catalog_quote: Any of the vowel phonemes may occur in either of the positions. Consonant length only occurs intervocalically. The glottal stop does not occur phonemically in initial position. Stress is rather pronounced, and falls most often on the penultimate syllable of the root word. Since stress placement is not affected by affixation, the root word will be separated from prefixes and suffixes with hyphens to assist the reader in identifying it. The Weyewa prefixes are pa-, ka-, ma-, and genitive and modal suffixes are -na, -ngge, -langge, -po, -ba, -do, and -ki; pronominal suffixes are -ngga, -nggu, -na, -ni, -ma, -nda, -mi(nggi), and -da. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is strong and regularly falls on the penultimate syllable of the root; prefixes (pa-, ka-, ma-) and suffixes/enclitics (-na, -ngge, -nggu, etc.) do not shift it, so stress stays on the root penult in affixed words (pa-kawúkku-na). A few lexical exceptions have antepenultimate stress (wátara 'corn'). Kuipers treats consonant length, not stress or vowel length, as the contrastive prosodic feature; penult vowels are laxed/shortened before geminate consonants.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical exceptions exist, e.g. wátara 'corn' (antepenultimate); 'falls most often' on the root penult. Kuipers 1990: xxiii also notes only 'lenis stress' occurs in monosyllables (pu 'heart', du 'connection').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the root word: affixation (prefixes and pronominal/genitive/modal suffixes) does not affect stress placement. Statement is an orthographic/phonological note prefacing an ethnography of ritual speech, based on Kuipers' fieldwork in the Weyewa highlands (west Sumba); dialect variation noted for segments (Laura, Tana Righu, near Loli) but not for stress. Consistent with Lovestrand 2021:48 (stressed, typically penultimate, vowels lengthened non-contrastively; citing Kuipers 1998: xvii) and Grimes & Edwards 2026:141 (Sumba languages: penultimate root stress, epenthetic final vowel extrametrical, e.g. Weyewa tazik-a).
new_statements.identity_note: Kuipers describes 'Weyewa' as spoken in the Weyewa highlands of west Sumba (Wewewa proper), matching weje1237 [wew]; he notes segmental dialect variation in Laura/Loura (Glottolog sometimes separate, nucl1519 / ISO lur) and Tana Righu (tana1282) but the stress statement is given for Weyewa generally. Bulu 2018 (not seen) describes the Weekombaka (Wewewa Barat) variety.
